conventions.convention: Rademacher complexity uses the one-sided sign supremum, normalization 1/m, and no absolute value; the class is nonempty but need not contain zero.
Expected complexity requires measurability of the sign supremum on the sample space; no completeness assumption on the probability space is imposed.

Coordinate contraction applies to real-valued classes with finite sign suprema, using finite/countable classes or a specified countable subclass preserving both suprema for every sign vector. The common Lipschitz constant may be zero; maps need not vanish at zero.

The four uniform generalization bounds are separate probability guarantees. AC and measurability of the relevant sample, ghost-sample, and sign suprema for both the class and its complement class are assumed.
The approximate ERM rule is assumed to exist, belong to the hypothesis class on every sample, and have measurable selected population risk; the approximation tolerance is fixed and finite.

load_bearing.statement: For a nonempty measurable [0,1]-valued class and m≥1, empirical complexity is the uniform sign average of sup_g m⁻¹Σ_i σ_i g(z_i); expected complexity averages this statistic over an IID sample when the displayed supremum is measurable.

Under AC and the stated bounded-class and measurability hypotheses, each guarantee holds separately with probability at least 1−δ: Pg≤P_mg+2R_m+√(log(1/δ)/(2m)) uniformly in g; Pg≤P_mg+2R̂_S+3√(log(2/δ)/(2m)) uniformly in g; sup_g|Pg−P_mg|≤2R_m+√(log(2/δ)/(2m)); sup_g|Pg−P_mg|≤2R̂_S+3√(log(4/δ)/(2m)).

For a nonempty measurable [0,1]-valued class, an IID sample of size m≥1, an independent IID copy, independent uniform signs, and the stated measurable suprema, E_S sup_g(Pg−P_mg)≤2R_m(G). No choice axiom is assumed.

For a fixed sample, common L-Lipschitz coordinate maps with L≥0, and a nonempty real-valued class satisfying the stated countable-reduction and finite-supremum hypotheses, m⁻¹E_σ sup_hΣ_iσ_iΦ_i(h(z_i))≤L R̂_S(H). No condition Φ_i(0)=0 is required.

concerns.concern: The Definition says: “a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices.” This does not ensure the required measurability on the stated, potentially incomplete probability space. Counterexample: take [0,1] with its Borel sigma-algebra and Borel Lebesgue probability, a non-Borel subset A of the null Cantor set, m=1, and G={0}∪{1_{ {a} }:a∈A}. Every member is Borel measurable. For each sign, the supremum agrees with that over the countable subclass {0} outside the Cantor set. Nevertheless the positive-sign supremum is 1_A and empirical complexity is 1_A/2, neither Borel measurable. The asserted sufficient condition requires an explicit measurable-version or completion convention, or stronger equality.

seams_checked.note: This is a contextual page prerequisite rather than an invocation of a finite-class PAC theorem. The ERM corollary uses the actual approximate-ERM definition, explicitly assumes class membership and selector existence, and does not impose finiteness or claim attainment.

The direct comparison example ex-stability-versus-training-accuracy-and-rademacher-bound uses the one-sided 1/m convention and the two-sided expected-complexity bound with log(2/δ), retaining AC and measurable finite-class hypotheses. Its m=1 complexity is correctly 1/2.

The prerequisite is contextual. The population adaptation results do not invoke a Rademacher theorem; their source commentary explicitly separates empirical discrepancy estimates and their additional Rademacher and bounded-loss hypotheses.

lem-empirical-rademacher-covering-integral and lem-multiclass-margin-rademacher-generalization preserve the one-sided 1/n convention for [0,1]-valued classes. The latter independently proves measurable countable reduction and the empirical one-sided bound with coefficient 3 and log(2/δ), carrying AC.

The latent-class definition explicitly distinguishes its unnormalized vector complexity. lem-contrastive-uniform-generalization normalizes the bounded loss to [0,1], retains AC and measurable suprema, and quotes the two-sided empirical bound with log(4/δ). Its proof restores the loss oscillation and 1/M factors correctly.
